name: Customer support
summary: Customer support interviews, including BPO and call-centre hiring, usually focus on how you communicate and how you treat an upset customer. Candidates commonly report a short HR screen, a spoken-English, voice or typing test depending on whether the job is on calls, chat or email, and an operations round with role-plays of difficult conversations. Technical support roles add basic troubleshooting questions.
rounds: HR screen on your background, availability and communication
Communication test: spoken English or a voice test for call roles, typing or writing for chat and email roles (often online)
Operations or team-leader round with role-plays of customer calls or chats
For technical support, questions on basic troubleshooting of devices, apps or networks
Final HR discussion on shifts, location and joining (for many roles)
looks_for: Clear, polite and calm speech or writing
Listening fully before answering, and checking you've understood
Empathy that leads to a solution, not just an apology
Following the process while still owning the customer's problem
Comfort with targets such as handling time, resolution rate and satisfaction scores
Reliability: shifts, attendance and staying steady when it's busy

questions.text: Tell me about a time you helped someone who was angry or upset. What did you say?
covers: Why they were upset, in a sentence
What you said and did to calm things and fix the problem
How it ended and what you learned

questions.text: Tell me about a time you couldn't give someone what they wanted. How did you handle it?
covers: What they asked for and why you couldn't do it
How you explained it kindly and what you offered instead
How they reacted in the end

questions.text: Describe a time you went out of your way to solve a problem for someone, at work, college or home.
covers: The problem and why it mattered to them
The extra step you took
The result for them

questions.text: Tell me about feedback you've had on how you communicate. What did you change?
covers: The feedback, stated honestly
What you changed, such as pace, clarity or tone
A sign that it worked

questions.text: A customer calls, shouting that their order is late for the third time. Walk me through how you'd handle the call.
covers: Letting them finish, then acknowledging the problem in your own words
Checking the facts and saying clearly what you can do and by when
Following up as promised and noting the case so they don't have to repeat it

questions.text: Let's role-play: I'm a customer whose refund hasn't arrived. Start the call.
covers: A proper greeting and checking who the customer is
Questions to find the order and the problem
A clear next step, a timeline and a polite close

questions.text: What are first-contact resolution and average handling time, and what goes wrong if you chase only one of them?
covers: Resolution: solving it in one contact; handling time: how long each contact takes
Rushing calls to cut time makes customers call back
Balancing both, with quality as the aim

questions.text: A customer asks for something that's against company policy. What would you do?
covers: Explaining the policy simply, without blaming anyone
Offering what you can do instead
Escalating to a senior if the case is unusual

questions.text: A customer keeps asking to speak to a supervisor. How would you handle it?
covers: Trying once more to understand and solve the problem yourself
Escalating politely if they still want it, following the process
Passing on the details so the customer doesn't start again

questions.text: Your queue is long and calls are back to back. How do you stay accurate and calm?
covers: Treating each customer as the only one on that call
Using notes, templates and the knowledge base to avoid mistakes
Short resets between calls and asking for help when needed

questions.text: How would you explain a simple fix, like restarting a router or updating an app, to someone who isn't comfortable with technology?
covers: One step at a time, in plain words, without jargon
Checking after each step that it worked
Patience, and offering another way if they get stuck

questions.text: A user says their laptop has become very slow. Which questions would you ask first?
covers: When it started and whether anything changed, such as an update or new software
Basic checks: a restart, free storage, programs running in the background
When you'd escalate to a higher level of support

questions.text: How do you write a good reply to a complaint on chat or email?
covers: Acknowledging the problem and using the customer's name
A clear answer or next step in short sentences
Checking tone and spelling, and that you answered every point
Your education or work in two lines
Something that shows you communicate well or like helping people
Why this job now

questions.text: What does good customer service mean to you?
covers: Solving the problem, not just being polite
An example of good service you received or gave
How you'd bring that to this job

questions.text: Are you comfortable working night shifts, rotational shifts or weekends?
covers: An honest answer about your situation
How you'd manage sleep, travel and health on shifts
Any limits, stated clearly and early

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in two or three years if you join us?
covers: Growing in this job first: quality, scores, trust
A next step such as team leader, trainer, quality or a specialist queue
What you'd learn on the way

tips: Speak slowly and clearly; in a voice test, being easy to understand matters more than your accent.
In a role-play, use the customer's name, repeat their problem back and end with a clear next step.
Never blame another team or the customer; say what you can do.
Be honest about shifts, travel and location at the HR round; it saves trouble for both sides later.
For technical support, revise the basics: restarting, checking connections and settings, updates, and when to escalate.
For chat or email roles, practise typing short, correct replies quickly.
